content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Use titration to find unknown concentrations
is a precise technique for finding the concentration of an unknown solution. It involves measuring exactly how much of one solution is needed to react completely with a known volume of another.
A technique to find the exact volume of one solution needed to react completely with a known volume of another solution.
The point at which the indicator changes colour, showing the reaction is complete.
The point of exact neutralisation (may differ slightly from endpoint).
[DIAGRAM: Titration setup showing burette clamped vertically above conical flask on white tile, with flask containing alkali and indicator]
Measures variable volume of acid (to 0.1 cm³)
Measures fixed volume of alkali (to 0.1 cm³)
Makes colour change easier to see
Use pipette and filler to measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali
Transfer to a clean conical flask
Add 2-3 drops of indicator (e.g., methyl orange or phenolphthalein)
Run some out to fill the tip and set to 0.00 cm³
Add acid from burette, swirling flask constantly
Stop when indicator just changes colour permanently
Volume used = Final reading - Initial reading
Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000
Calculate moles of the known solution
Use the equation ratio to find moles of unknown
25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.
25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide was neutralised by 30.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Calculate the concentration of potassium hydroxide.
What volume of 0.5 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is needed to neutralise 20.0 cm³ of 0.25 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide?
Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³
Using all titration values in the mean
Only use concordant values; discard anomalies
Forgetting to use the equation ratio
Check the balanced equation - ratios are not always 1:1
Describe how you would carry out a titration of hydrochloric acid against sodium hydroxide solution. (6 marks)
a) Identify any anomalous results. (1 mark)
b) Calculate the mean titre. (2 marks)
25.0 cm³ of NaOH was neutralised by 22.5 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl. Calculate the concentration of NaOH. (4 marks)
What volume of 0.2 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ is needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 0.4 mol/dm³ NaOH? (4 marks)
Explain why concordant results are important in titrations. (2 marks)
Why is phenolphthalein unsuitable for titrating a strong acid with a weak alkali? (2 marks)
